threads.thread_goal: Align on target layouts, measurements, and main constraints for the kitchen line.

messages.text: Team, let's kick off the 'Standardized Custom Kitchen Line for Small Apartments' project. First step is T1: Define standard layouts and measurements. I've started a document for this, A1. The goal is to agree on a few core layouts we can design our modules for. Let's start by brainstorming the most common kitchen shapes we see in small apartments.
Great. I can start. Most are just a single wall, or sometimes an L-shape. I've seen a few with two walls opposite each other too. I can sketch these up and put them in A1 right away.
What do you mean two walls opposite? like a hallway?

Yes, that's often called a 'galley' kitchen. Good point @45878, those three cover most cases. While we're defining layouts in A1, we should also think about the measurement checklist. We need to include appliance dimensions, but also access paths like doorway widths and tight corners in stairwells. I can add a section for that based on my moving experience.

That's a critical point, @495992. On-site access is a major constraint. Please add that to the checklist structure in A1. So, the three layouts are: 1. Single-Wall (I-Shape), 2. L-Shape, 3. Galley. Does everyone agree these are the right ones to focus on for V1?

Apologies for the delay. Those three layouts are the industry standard for this segment and a solid choice. Focusing on them allows us to standardize plumbing and electrical placement assumptions, which simplifies module design. The access checklist from @495992 is also essential to prevent on-site rework.
Yep, sounds good to me. I'll wait for the green light and then update A1 with the final layout sketches.
ok

Perfect, we have alignment. Let's formalize the decisions.
Decision: We will support I-Shape, L-Shape, and Galley layouts for V1.0.
Decision: The measurement checklist in A1 will include a section for on-site access constraints (doorways, stairs).

threads.thread_goal: Define the initial modular cabinet set, cut lists, and compatible finishes.

messages.text: Hi all, I've created the first draft of the module designs and cut lists in A2, as part of T2. I've added a few standard base and wall cabinet sizes (600mm, 800mm). Take a look and let me know what you think.
Thanks! Looking at A2 now. Did we consider a corner cabinet module for the L-shape layouts? We'll definitely need one.

Good catch, @495992. We'll need a standard blind corner or a 90-degree corner unit. Also, looking at the base cabinet depth in A2, 600mm is standard but it doesn't leave much room for plumbing behind. I suggest we reduce the cabinet box depth to 580mm to give installers 20mm of play. We should also add a tall pantry module, maybe 600mm wide, as that's a common request for storage.
What about a 750mm wide cabinet? I had a client who wanted one of those once.

While custom sizes are possible, the goal here is standardization to make production repeatable and efficient. We should stick to a limited set of common sizes for V1. The 580mm depth is a smart adjustment, @82913. While we're on standards, we should discuss T4 and define finishes. I've started a draft for A4. Based on current trends, I propose we start with two options for the prototype: a 'Natural Oak' veneer and a 'Matte White' lacquer. They are popular, durable, and we have reliable suppliers for both.

I like those finish options. Easy to work with. I've updated A2 with the 580mm depth, a blind corner base, and a 600mm wide tall pantry. I also added the two finishes to the A4 draft. Is this list good for the prototype?

This looks like a solid, versatile set for the prototype. Let's lock it in. 
Decision: The module list for the prototype will be as specified in the latest version of A2 (including standard, corner, and tall units).
Decision: The prototype will use two finishes: 'Natural Oak' and 'Matte White', as documented in A4.

threads.thread_goal: Plan and track the prototype build in the workshop, including quality checks.

messages.text: Alright team, the cut lists in A2 are locked. It's time to start the prototype build for T3. Let's plan the workshop sequence. Who wants to take the lead on different stages?
I can get started on cutting all the panels from the lists in A2 this morning.

Before you start, let's all do a quick review of the safety guidelines in A8. For workflow, I suggest we batch the process for efficiency: 1. Cut all panels. 2. Edge-band all required edges. 3. Drill all panels for hardware and joinery. 4. Assemble boxes. This will be faster than each of us building one cabinet from start to finish.
when do we make the drawers?

We can build the drawers while the main box assembly is happening. But it's a good idea to build one drawer and test-fit it in one of the first cabinet boxes to make sure our tolerances and hardware settings are perfect before making all of them.

Good thinking. Now, let's talk quality. Per T8, we need a solid QC process. I've started the checklist in A3. What are the non-negotiable checks we must perform in the workshop before the modules are wrapped for transport?
Final dimensions must match A2.
Check that all cabinets are square.
And a thorough visual inspection of the finish under proper lighting. No scratches, no drips, consistent color. This is what the customer sees first.

Excellent. Let's lock that in. 
Decision: We will follow the batched build sequence: Cut -> Edge-band -> Drill -> Assemble.
Decision: The mandatory pre-transport QC checks are: 1. Critical dimensions vs. A2, 2. Cabinet squareness, 3. Final finish quality. I'll update A3 accordingly.

threads.thread_goal: Align on packaging, loading, and on-site handling for the prototype install.

messages.text: Update: All prototype modules are built and have passed the workshop QC checks listed in A3. They're ready for finishing touches and then we can plan transport (T5, T6).

Perfect timing. I've drafted a packaging procedure in A5. My proposal is to use heavy-duty cardboard corner protectors on all edges, wrap the body in 3 layers of stretch wrap, and add a 5mm foam sheet over any door or drawer fronts to protect the finish. This should be robust enough for transport.

That's a solid foundation. Two additions from my experience: First, we must tape all doors and drawers securely shut with low-tack painter's tape. Second, for the loading plan in T6, we need to use a 'last in, first out' strategy. The items needed first on site (base cabinets) should be loaded last into the van, so they are easy to access. Wall cabinets and tall units should be loaded first.
can we just put them on a pallet?

A pallet won't fit through apartment building hallways or elevators, which is a key constraint of this project. The individual wrapping proposed by @495992 and refined by @506532 is the right approach. The loading order is also a crucial detail that will save a lot of time and hassle on site.
Good points. I've updated A5 to include taping doors/drawers and to specify the loading order. It should be ready for final review.
Looks complete now. Let's make it official. Decision: We approve the standard packaging method (corner protectors, wrap, foam, tape) and the 'last in, first out' loading order as documented in A5.

threads.thread_goal: Review the test apartment installation and close version 1.0 of the standard.

messages.text: Team, the prototype installation for T7 is complete. Fantastic work getting it done. I've written up the full installation report, with photos of the finished kitchen and notes on issues we encountered, in A7. Please review it so we can finalize the V1.0 standard (T12).
It looks great! The install was pretty smooth. I've already logged the build and install times in A6 to get a head start on T9. I can also get the photos ready for the sales pack for T10.

I'm reviewing A7. One significant issue was fitting the cabinets against the back wall, which wasn't perfectly plumb. The filler strip we had to cut on-site was time-consuming. For the final standard, I strongly recommend we add a standard, oversized scribe panel to the cut list. We can ship a 100mm wide strip with every order and the installer can rip it to the exact size needed on site. It will produce a much cleaner result.

I agree, that was a pain point. Another thing I noticed during the install was adjusting the leveling legs at the back of the base cabinets. Once the cabinet was against the wall, they were almost impossible to reach. We should research alternative hardware - there are legs that can be adjusted with a screwdriver from inside the cabinet.
so we have to change the whole design?

Not at all. These are exactly the kinds of refinements the prototype process is meant to uncover. They are small changes to the standard that will make every future installation much faster and better. The suggestions from @506532 and @495992 are excellent. Are there any other major changes needed before we finalize V1.0?
No, those two seem like the big ones. The rest worked well.

Okay, let's decide. Decision: The final V1.0 standard will be updated with two changes based on the prototype install: 1. Addition of a standard oversized scribe panel to the module set. 2. Specification of front-adjustable leveling legs for all base cabinets.

With that, we can close out T12. @506532, can you please add the scribe panel to A2? @495992, please research the new leg hardware and add the spec to A2. @45878, please finalize the photo pack for T10. I will consolidate all final documents. Great work everyone.
